In the [previous post](../random-variables/index.qmd) we saw that a random variable $X$ sends each outcome of an experiment to a number, and that $P(X = x)$ is the probability of all the outcomes that lead to the value $x$. When $X$ is discrete, these probabilities, one for each value, describe its distribution completely. The function that collects them is the **probability mass function**.

## Definition and properties

The **probability mass function** (pmf) of a discrete random variable $X$ is the function $f_X : \mathbb{R} \to [0, 1]$ given by

$$f_X(x) = P(X = x).$$

Every pmf has two properties:

1. $0 \le f_X(x) \le 1$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}$,
2. $\displaystyle\sum_x f_X(x) = 1$, where the sum runs over all values of $X$.

The converse also holds: any function with these two properties on a finite or countable set of values is the pmf of some discrete random variable. The pmf is also written $p_X(x)$, or just $f(x)$ or $p(x)$ when there is no risk of confusion. The word "mass" is used only for discrete random variables: probability sits on isolated points, like point masses. The corresponding notion for continuous random variables is the probability **density** function.

From the pmf we can compute the probability of **any** event involving $X$: add up the mass of the values that belong to it,

$$P(X \in B) = \sum_{x \in B} f_X(x).$$

**Example.** For the result of rolling a die, $f_X(x) = 1/6$ for $x = 1, 2, \ldots, 6$ and $f_X(x) = 0$ for any other $x$. The probability of rolling at least 5 is $f_X(5) + f_X(6) = 1/3$.

## Is it a pmf? Two examples

**Example 1.** We show that

$$f(x) = \frac{1}{4} \left( \frac{3}{4} \right)^x, \quad x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$

is a pmf. The first property holds since $0 < f(x) \le 1/4$. For the second we use the geometric series $\sum_{x \ge 0} q^x = 1/(1 - q)$ for $|q| < 1$:

$$\sum_{x=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{4} \left( \frac{3}{4} \right)^x = \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - 3/4} = 1.$$

If $X$ has this pmf, then

$$P(0 \le X \le 3) = \frac{1}{4} \left( 1 + \frac{3}{4} + \frac{9}{16} + \frac{27}{64} \right) = 1 - \left( \frac{3}{4} \right)^4 = \frac{175}{256} \approx 0.684.$$

This pmf is positive at infinitely many values, which decrease quickly. $X$ counts, for example, the failures before the first success in repeated trials with success probability $1/4$: for $X = x$, the first $x$ trials must fail and the next one succeed.

**Example 2.** For which constant $c$ is $f(x) = c x^2$, $x = 1, 2, 3$, a pmf? From the second property:

$$c \cdot 1 + c \cdot 4 + c \cdot 9 = 14c = 1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad c = \frac{1}{14}.$$

With $c = 1/14$ the first property holds as well, since the values $1/14$, $4/14$, $9/14$ all lie in $[0, 1]$. The constant that makes the sum equal to 1 is called the **normalising constant**.

## A probability calculator for a pmf

Pick a function and an event. The bars in the event are coloured, and its probability is the sum of their heights. For $c x^2$, move the slider and watch the check on the second property: only one value of $c$ gives a pmf.

Probability mass function and probabilities of events
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
pmfs32 = new Map([
  ["Die: f(x) = 1/6, x = 1, …, 6", {id: "die"}],
  ["f(x) = (1/4)(3/4)^x, x = 0, 1, 2, …", {id: "geo"}],
  ["f(x) = c·x², x = 1, 2, 3", {id: "cx2"}],
  ["Fans: number among 3 residents, p = 0.8", {id: "fans"}],
  ["f(x) = 2^(−x), x = 1, 2, 3, …", {id: "half"}]
])
viewof d32 = Inputs.select(pmfs32, {label: "Function"})
viewof k32 = Inputs.range([5, 30], {step: 1, value: 10, label: "For c·x² only: c = 1/k, k ="})
viewof ev32 = Inputs.radio(["a ≤ X ≤ b", "X even", "X odd", "X multiple of 3"], {value: "a ≤ X ≤ b", label: "Event"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
sup32 = {
  const id = d32.id, bin = (n, k) => k < 0 || k > n ? 0 : [...Array(k).keys()].reduce((t, i) => t * (n - i) / (i + 1), 1);
  if (id === "die") return {xs: d3.range(1, 7), f: x => 1 / 6, shown: 6, inf: false};
  if (id === "geo") return {xs: d3.range(0, 120), f: x => 0.25 * 0.75 ** x, shown: 16, inf: true};
  if (id === "cx2") return {xs: [1, 2, 3], f: x => x * x / k32, shown: 3, inf: false};
  if (id === "fans") return {xs: [0, 1, 2, 3], f: x => bin(3, x) * 0.8 ** x * 0.2 ** (3 - x), shown: 4, inf: false};
  return {xs: d3.range(1, 120), f: x => 2 ** -x, shown: 15, inf: true};
}
viewof ab32 = {
  const xs = sup32.xs.slice(0, sup32.shown), lo = xs[0], hi = xs[xs.length - 1];
  const a = Inputs.range([lo, hi], {step: 1, value: lo, label: "a"});
  const b = Inputs.range([lo, hi], {step: 1, value: Math.min(hi, lo + 3), label: "b"});
  const wrap = html`<div>${ev32 === "a ≤ X ≤ b" ? html`${a}${b}` : html``}</div>`;
  Object.defineProperty(wrap, "value", {get: () => [a.value, b.value]});
  a.addEventListener("input", () => wrap.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true})));
  b.addEventListener("input", () => wrap.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true})));
  return wrap;
}
```


With the pmf $(1/4)(3/4)^x$ and $a = 0$, $b = 3$ you get the $0.684$ of Example 1. For $c x^2$, $k = 14$ is the only setting whose sum is 1. The "Fans" option is the example that follows.

## From the sample space to the pmf

80% of the residents of a town support the local football team. We pick 3 residents at random and let $X$ = {the number who support the team}. To find the pmf of $X$ we start, as in the previous post, from the sample space. Writing S for a supporter and N for a non-supporter, there are 8 outcomes, from SSS to NNN. The choices are independent, so e.g. $P(\text{SNS}) = 0.8 \cdot 0.2 \cdot 0.8 = 0.128$. Grouping by value:

| $x$ | Outcomes with $X = x$ | $f_X(x)$ |
|:-:|:-|:-:|
| 0 | NNN | $0.2^3 = 0.008$ |
| 1 | SNN, NSN, NNS | $3 \cdot 0.8 \cdot 0.2^2 = 0.096$ |
| 2 | SSN, SNS, NSS | $3 \cdot 0.8^2 \cdot 0.2 = 0.384$ |
| 3 | SSS | $0.8^3 = 0.512$ |

The values add up to 1. The form $\binom{3}{x} 0.8^x\, 0.2^{3-x}$ is the **binomial distribution**, which will get a post of its own.

## In R

In R a pmf with finitely many values is just two vectors: the values and their probabilities. With them we check the properties, compute probabilities and run simulations.

```{r}
#| label: pmf-r
x <- 1:3
f <- x^2 / 14
c(all_in_01 = all(f >= 0 & f <= 1), total = sum(f))
# P(X >= 2)
sum(f[x >= 2])
# 10,000 draws of X and their relative frequencies
sims <- sample(x, 10000, replace = TRUE, prob = f)
round(table(sims) / 10000, 3)
```

With infinitely many values we sum enough terms. R has the pmf of Example 1 built in: it is `dgeom(x, prob = 1/4)`.

```{r}
#| label: geo-r
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of the pmf f(x) = (1/4)(3/4)^x for x from 0 to 20. The bars decrease geometrically, with the values 0 to 3 highlighted."
x <- 0:20
f <- 0.25 * 0.75^x
all.equal(f, dgeom(x, prob = 0.25))
# P(0 <= X <= 3)
sum(f[x <= 3])
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
barplot(f, names.arg = x, col = ifelse(x <= 3, "#f28e2b", "#4e79a7"),
        border = NA, xlab = "x", ylab = "f(x)", las = 1)
```

The sum of the first four terms is `r fmt(sum(0.25 * 0.75^(0:3)), 4)`, the $175/256$ we found above.

## Summary

- The pmf of a discrete r.v. is $f_X(x) = P(X = x)$.
- Any function with $0 \le f(x) \le 1$ and $\sum_x f(x) = 1$ is a pmf. The second property pins down unknown constants.
- $P(X \in B) = \sum_{x \in B} f_X(x)$: the probability of an event is the mass that lies in it.
- To find the pmf of an r.v., start from the sample space and group the outcomes by value.

## Review questions

**1. Quick quiz.**

::: {.ix-panel}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
quiz32 = [
  {q: "Which of these is a pmf on the values x = 1, 2, 3, 4?",
   opts: ["f(x) = x/10", "f(x) = x/4", "f(x) = (x − 2)/2", "f(x) = 1/3"], ans: 0,
   why: "1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, so x/10 sums to 1. x/4 sums to 2.5, (x − 2)/2 is negative at x = 1 and 1/3 sums to 4/3."},
  {q: "If f(x) = c·(1/2)^x for x = 0, 1, 2, …, what is c?",
   opts: ["1", "1/2", "2", "1/4"], ans: 1,
   why: "Σ (1/2)^x = 1/(1 − 1/2) = 2, so 2c = 1 and c = 1/2."},
  {q: "X has f(0) = 0.2, f(1) = 0.5, f(2) = 0.3. What is P(X ≠ 1)?",
   opts: ["0.5", "0.3", "0.2", "0.7"], ans: 0,
   why: "P(X ≠ 1) = 1 − f(1) = 0.5, or equivalently f(0) + f(2) = 0.2 + 0.3."},
  {q: "Can a pmf have f(x) > 0 for infinitely many x?",
   opts: ["No, the sum would be infinite", "Yes, as long as the sum is 1", "Only if X is continuous"], ans: 1,
   why: "E.g. (1/4)(3/4)^x is positive for every x = 0, 1, 2, … and sums to 1. The terms just have to decrease fast enough."}
]
{
  const root = html`<div></div>`, score = html`<div class="ix-note"></div>`, done = new Map();
  quiz32.forEach((item, k) => {
    const fb = html`<div class="ix-note"></div>`;
    const btns = item.opts.map(o => html`<button>${o}</button>`);
    const opts = html`<div style="margin:4px 0 0 6px">${btns.map((b, j) => {
      b.onclick = () => {
        const ok = j === item.ans; done.set(k, ok);
        btns.forEach(x => x.className = "");
        b.className = ok ? "ix-picked-ok" : "ix-picked-no";
        fb.innerHTML = (ok ? `<span class="ix-ok">✓ Correct.</span> ` : `<span class="ix-no">✗ Not quite.</span> `) + item.why;
        score.innerHTML = `<b>Correct: ${[...done.values()].filter(x => x).length} of ${quiz32.length}</b>`;
      };
      return b;
    })}</div>`;
    root.append(html`<div style="margin:12px 0"><div>${k + 1}. ${item.q}</div>${opts}${fb}</div>`);
  });
  root.append(score);
  return root;
}
```

**2.** The discrete r.v. $X$ has pmf $f_X(x) = 2^{-x}$, $x = 1, 2, \ldots$

(a) Is $X$ more likely to take an even or an odd value?
(b) Compute $P(X > 5)$ and $P(X \text{ is divisible by } 3)$.

Check your answers in the calculator, with the function $2^{-x}$.

**3.** Find the constant $c$ such that $f(x) = c\,(x + 1)$, $x = 0, 1, 2, 3$, is a pmf, and compute $P(X \ge 2)$.

**4.** Two dice are rolled and $X$ = {the absolute difference of the results}. Find the pmf of $X$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

2. (a) $P(X \text{ odd}) = \sum_{k \ge 1} 2^{-(2k-1)} = \dfrac{1/2}{1 - 1/4} = \dfrac{2}{3}$, so $P(X \text{ even}) = 1/3$. An odd value is more likely, mainly because $x = 1$ alone has probability $1/2$.
(b) $P(X > 5) = \sum_{x \ge 6} 2^{-x} = 2^{-5} = 1/32$. $P(X \text{ is divisible by } 3) = \sum_{k \ge 1} 2^{-3k} = \dfrac{1/8}{1 - 1/8} = \dfrac{1}{7}$.
3. $c\,(1 + 2 + 3 + 4) = 10c = 1$, so $c = 1/10$ and $P(X \ge 2) = (3 + 4)/10 = 0.7$.
4. $X$ takes the values $0, 1, \ldots, 5$ with $f_X(0) = 6/36$ and $f_X(k) = 2(6 - k)/36$ for $k = 1, \ldots, 5$, i.e. $6/36, 10/36, 8/36, 6/36, 4/36, 2/36$, which add up to 1.
:::
